Chapter 1: Childhood in Vienna—Family, Dreams, and the Shadow of Change
Imagine growing up in Vienna, a city alive with music drifting from open windows and neighbors chatting on every street corner. Back then, everything felt wide open—like the world was just waiting for you to step out and make your mark. In the middle of it all, there’s a young girl, part of a family that truly cherished learning and tradition. Her mother, always calm and steady, kept their home running with loving care, while her father—a well-respected lawyer—sparked her curiosity and encouraged her to dream big.
Their Jewish heritage? It wasn’t something they wore for the world to see. It was just quietly woven into their daily lives—a source of belonging and gentle pride.
School felt like a place where just about anything was possible. This girl, bright and determined, wanted nothing more than to follow in her father’s footsteps and become a lawyer herself. She spent her afternoons giggling with friends, sharing secrets and laughter, never once thinking that something dark could reach into their happy corner of the world. Vienna, with its beautiful parks and grand old buildings, felt safe—a city that promised a bright future.
But even then, there were little signs that not everyone felt welcome. Sometimes, classmates would whisper hurtful things. Sometimes, a shopkeeper’s stare lingered just a bit too long. Most days, these moments were brushed aside—chalked up to ignorance or simple misunderstandings. It was easy to believe that if you just worked hard and showed kindness, you could push past any barrier.
As the 1930s rolled on, though, Vienna started to feel different. News from Germany got more alarming by the week. Political rallies, once just something you’d hear about, began filling the streets outside their door. The family would gather around the radio, listening in growing worry—but daily life kept moving forward. There were still birthdays to celebrate, exams to study for, and chores that needed doing. The idea that everything could change in a heartbeat? It just didn’t seem real.
And then, in 1938, the unimaginable became reality. The German army marched into Austria, and suddenly, the city erupted with celebration. Flags hung from windows, and neighbors—folks who’d always seemed friendly—cheered for the new regime. For Jewish families, everything got smaller in an instant. Rights vanished, one after another—first the right to work, then to study, then even to move freely. Her father lost his job. Friends stopped calling. The family’s savings drained away as they paid taxes and fines meant only for Jews.
That blanket of safety the family had always felt? It disappeared. Suddenly, fear crept into every conversation. Dreams for the future were replaced by anxious questions: Should we leave? Where could we possibly go? Is it safer to wait and hope, or to risk everything for a chance at escape?
This is when the true cost of being different came into sharp focus. What had once brought comfort now made the family a target. The girl watched her mother grow more anxious and her father more distant. She tried to hold onto her dreams, but the world just wasn’t making room for them anymore.
You know, most of us don’t notice when the ground starts shifting beneath our feet. It’s slow, until—suddenly—it isn’t. One day, you’re planning for tomorrow. The next, you’re just trying to make it through the day. For this family, and so many others, the Vienna they loved vanished overnight, replaced by a world where nothing was certain and survival became the only goal.
